item.title: Understanding activity spaces: Contemporary issues and challenges and future research directions
item.description:
Renee Zahnow, Jonathan Corcoran, Rebecca Wickes
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261492885
Activity spaces are a subset of locations where people spend their everyday lives. Interest in activity spaces spans the social sciences, geography, health sciences and transportation research. In recent years, the spread of smartphones and other tracking devices has made it far easier to record daily movements. This has sparked an increase in activity space research and an opportunity to consider how the concept has been conceptually and empirically defined over time and across disciplinary fields. In this scoping review, we analyse 372 studies of activity spaces published between 1972 and 2024. Despite conceptual consistency, we find that studies tend to focus, empirically, on one of four dimensions of activity spaces: access, nodes, paths and exposure. Drawing on our review, we suggest greater methodological harmonisation may better support replication and comparative studies and incremental research discovery. We propose that to achieve this, a more nuanced theoretical framework is required that defines each of the dimensions of activity space, how they are related to each other and incorporates aspects of daily activity in the new millennia (e.g. online, hybrid and multilayered time–space locations).

item.title: Bridging critical knowledge and action gaps in urban health: A call for transdisciplinary approaches in urban studies in the era of global population aging and climate change
item.description:
Vitor Pessoa Colombo, Elis Mina Seraya Borde, Mirko S. Winkler, Aline Dayrell Ferreira Sales, Amanda Cristina de Souza Andrade, Amanda Fernandes, Amanda Silva Magalhães, Amélia Augusta de Lima Friche, et al.
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261498090
Urbanization and population aging are two “mega-trends” posing significant challenges to global health, particularly under climate change. Despite extensive evidence on the links between the built environment and health, urban planning scholars and practitioners still miss valuable opportunities to contribute to public health and urban health equity—which often remain marginal or only implicit topics in urban planning discourses and practices. Against this background, we organized the transdisciplinary workshop “Global Health Challenges Related to Demographic & Climate Changes: Implications for Urban and Territorial Planning” (Basel, 2024), convening scholars and practitioners to co-develop a research agenda addressing knowledge-to-action gaps in urban health equity and climate resilience. Building on the workshop’s discussions, this commentary highlights current challenges in reconnecting urban planning and public health while presenting opportunities to bridge this gap. We argue for an “ultra-local” approach that acknowledges the chronic lack of granular data necessary to address spatial justice and urban health inequities, emphasizing the importance of evidence- and place-based planning. To illustrate this approach, we present two recent experiences: the BH-Viva project in Brazil, which assessed impact of slum-upgrading projects on urban health equity, and the Saint-Louis Master Plan in Senegal, a pioneering effort integrating climate resilience into urban policy and planning. Ultimately, we present what we identified as priority research paths in urban studies, having transdisciplinarity as a precondition for urban planners to effectively tackle pressing global health challenges.

item.title: Internationalization of progressive municipalism—Barcelona international relations strategies
item.description:
Agnieszka Szpak
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261498132
This article examines how the International Relations Master Plan 2020–2023 and the International Strategy 2025–2029 translate progressive municipalism into external action. Through qualitative content analysis and comparison, it identifies three mechanisms of internationalization: norm projection, networked amplification, and multilevel resource mobilization. Both Strategies promote a rights-based agenda centered on social justice, housing, democratic participation, digital rights, and ecological transition. However, the movement-oriented municipalism of the Colau administration has evolved under Collboni into a more institutionalized and partnership-based model. This shift demonstrates both the continuity and moderation of Barcelona’s progressive orientation. The article also highlights the limits of municipal internationalization: although the Strategies support agenda-setting, policy circulation, coalition-building, and access to resources, they neither confer formal international authority on the city nor guarantee implementation. Barcelona, therefore, illustrates both the potential and the structural constraints of cities seeking to influence state-centered international governance.

item.title: Build for whom? Contested state entrepreneurialism and the governance of affordable rental housing in Shanghai, China
item.description:
Qianyu Lu, Yang Song
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261498685
This paper critically interrogates state entrepreneurialism through an empirical analysis of China’s recent Affordable Rental Housing (ARH) programme. Prevailing accounts of social housing under neoliberalism tend to frame it as a residual, market-enabling instrument of welfare retrenchment. Such perspectives, however, inadequately capture contexts in which expanded provision is intertwined with intensified and reconfigured forms of state intervention. Drawing on 92 qualitative interviews in Shanghai, this paper shows how ARH operates as a strategically selective mechanism embedded within broader projects of labour governance and territorial development. While it functions as a spatial fix to absorb oversupplied housing stock amid the crisis tendencies of land-centred accumulation, its implementation reveals a fragmented and contested process of state entrepreneurialism. Intra-state frictions, bureaucratic negotiations and divergent local growth rationalities reproduce uneven and contingent outcomes, rather than a coherent developmental logic. Access to ARH is selectively structured to privilege skilled migrants, demonstrating how state housing provision is mobilised to sort labour and align welfare responsibilities with labour value extraction and urban competitiveness. Meanwhile, hierarchical state-market arrangements reproduce regulatory asymmetries and uneven access. This paper argues that social housing in contemporary China constitutes a contested terrain of accumulation and legitimation, complicating linear narratives of neoliberal convergence and advancing a more critical understanding of state-led housing provision.

item.title: Interpreting mobility reform through care: Ambivalent authority in Taiwan
item.description:
Francis Chia Hui Lin
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261498097
This article examines how human-centred mobility reform can reproduce, rather than displace, entrenched hierarchies of automobility. Focusing on Taiwan, it analyses a regulatory archive of national traffic legislation and Taipei municipal instruments through which recent safety reforms have been articulated in the language of care, participation, and protection for vulnerable road users. The article argues that these reforms do not simply replace vehicle-centred urban order with pedestrian-oriented governance. Instead, they overlay existing mobility hierarchies with increasingly dense classifications, conditional provisions, and delegated discretion. Drawing on Homi Bhabha’s concept of ambivalence, the paper conceptualises this condition as ambivalent authority: a mode of postcolonial governance in which authority must appear protective and non-coercive while preserving inherited infrastructures of motorised priority. Through analysis of human-oriented road design, pedestrian-priority legislation, scooter and non-motorised classifications, and municipal mechanisms for temporary road use, the paper shows how care becomes a territorial technology of rule. Its contribution is threefold: it links postcolonial theory to urban mobility governance, clarifies how automobility persists through reform rather than only through resistance to reform, and reframes regulatory complexity as a political mechanism through which contradictory urban priorities are managed. The article concludes that mobility reform in Taiwan governs not by resolving the tension between care and hierarchy, but by continually recalibrating it.

item.title: From Frankenstein to Gulliver urbanism: Reframing AI and scale in urban theory
item.description:
Farshad Shariatpour
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261473549
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in urban governance, infrastructure and design, yet urban theory still lacks a clear language for analysing the scale asymmetries through which these systems operate. This article develops Gulliver Urbanism as a conceptual framework for understanding how AI reshapes urban power when it processes information, acts, and coordinates across cognitive, temporal and spatial horizons that exceed ordinary human capacities and institutional rhythms. Moving beyond Frankenstein Urbanism’s emphasis on rebellion and loss of control, we argue that the central problem of contemporary AI urbanism is scale asymmetry within co-constituted human and machine assemblages. The framework comprises six dimensions: cognitive scale, temporal scale, spatial scale, governance asymmetry, autonomy and agency and human response. It synthesises scholarship on AI urbanism, urban political economy, infrastructural urbanism, posthumanism, law and scale, supported by AI governance frameworks and vignettes on Hangzhou City Brain, robotaxis and generative design. The article conceptualises the urban as a constitutive condition of AI scale asymmetry, where algorithmic systems encounter infrastructure, land, mobility, public services, municipal authority, social difference and collective life. Across these domains, the key challenge is how to govern systems whose capacities outpace human oversight while remaining embedded in corporate, legal and political arrangements. We argue that effective responses require mixed-intelligence governance and temporal dignity: arrangements that subject algorithmic operations to democratic oversight, contestation and human-paced deliberation. Gulliver Urbanism explains how AI reconstitutes urban life by reorganising infrastructures, municipal authority, spatial relations, design imaginaries, public services and everyday citizenship.

item.title: Beyond the perimeter walls: Negotiated porosity and the governance of megaproject edges in Metro Manila
item.description:
Justin D. Stern
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261498686
This article examines Bonifacio Global City (BGC), an urban megaproject in Metro Manila, from the perspective of two adjacent barangays, or local government units: Guadalupe Nuevo and South Cembo. Drawing on fieldwork conducted between 2017 and 2024, it asks how these barangays manage the demands of a megaproject planned and marketed as self-contained, and how interdependence at the enclave edge becomes a basis for contesting the terms of urban porosity. Like many central business districts, BGC does not house many of the workers its economy depends on; it relies in part on adjacent barangays that provide the lower-cost housing, everyday services and mobility connections many workers require. The closure and later negotiated reopening of the J.P. Rizal butas, a long-standing informal opening in BGC’s perimeter wall, made this interdependence politically visible. From this case, the paper develops the concept of negotiated porosity. The term describes how the dependencies that sustain an enclave can become spatially concentrated at an interruptible point on its edge, allowing local government actors to contest the status and terms of access across the boundary. The article contributes to work on enclave urbanism, porous enclaves and the governance of urban megaprojects in the Philippines and beyond.

item.title: Cultural buffering in entrepreneurial city diplomacy: Wuxi’s economic engagement abroad
item.description:
Yichao Du
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261500009
Why do investment-oriented municipal delegations begin with culture? This article develops cultural buffering to explain how municipal actors use cultural forms and assets when development-oriented diplomacy brings together organisations with different authority, timetables and commitments. The analysis draws on multi-sited ethnography of 5 Wuxi delegation circuits across Japan, the United Kingdom and continental Europe, followed by tracing of 21 initiatives to July 2026. It identifies two recurrent problems: municipal schedules can outrun partner learning and due diligence, while demands for visible outputs can exceed commitment and post-event ownership. Municipal actors respond to these temporal and accountability mismatches through naming, sequencing, coalition broadening and managed ambiguity. These moves can change who participates, what becomes discussable, which organisations enter the relationship and how provisional alignment is recorded. Subsequent project implementation depends on authority, resources, delivery capacity and an organisation willing to own the next step. Cultural buffering therefore identifies the encounter-level work through which an unsettled proposal becomes discussable and revisitable before its implementation is determined.

item.title: Narrating ontologies of ruination in the disciplinary blur: Ruins as temporal gardens, trees as legal witnesses and birds as world-makers
item.description:
Mariya Hamada
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261500245
This commentary investigates the disciplinary blur that challenges the dual ontology of ruination as being both an urban/architectural transformation and an ecological phenomenon. It defies categorizations of objective knowledge and comes to terms with multispecies and interdisciplinary approaches, both historiographically and ethnographically, readjusting to the multiple temporalities of the nonhuman world-making projects that the human-made ruin becomes part of. Drawing on the urban ruin of 19 th -century Manchester (Cottonopolis), England, and the architectural ruins of contemporary Mogador, Morocco, it argues that the temporalities of the nonhuman, intersected respectively with periodicities of industrial contamination and human abandonment, transform the singular obsolete narrative of ruins into a plural transdisciplinary debate questioning the unyielding becoming of urban space. The text’s historiographical and ethnographical micronarratives, woven together through storytelling, theorize the transformative temporalities of urban nature and their capacity to provide the anthropogenic ruin with a collaborative ecological agency. This, the commentary argues, adds botanical and ornithological ontologies to urban and architectural taxonomies of ruination. By positioning oneself in the disciplinary blur, the commentary ideates on how architectural and urban studies can accommodate unfamiliar rhythms of nonhuman-constructed botanical and ornithological ruins.
